(0Day) (Pwn2Own) United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A OCPP UpdateFirmware Out-Of-Bounds Write Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
November 19th, 2026
ZDI-26-1038
ZDI-CAN-29487
CVE ID
CVE-2026-131813
CVSS Score
7.5
AV:A/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H
Affected Vendors
United Chargers
Affected Products
Grizzl-E Smart 40A
Vulnerability Details
This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.
The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP UpdateFirmware requests. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in a write past the end of an allocated buffer. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute code in the context of the device.
Additional Details
Since 04/14/26, ZDI has made multiple attempts to contact United Chargers to establish a vendor disclosure channel for the vulnerabilities identified in the Grizzl-E Smart 40A during Pwn2Own Automotive 2026. Despite these repeated efforts, both before and after the contest, the vendor has not responded to any communication.
-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

items.text: fushuling published: 硅基漫步：渗透智能体的过去和现在
items.title: 硅基漫步：渗透智能体的过去和现在
items.content:
前言
渗透智能体可能算是如今
AI for Secuirty
最火热的方向，甚至可以没有之一，从去年年底的第一次腾讯 AI 渗透大赛，当时还是做的 XBow 这样的 CTF 型的题目，到今年百花齐放，百度、字节等各家都在办自己的 AI 渗透大赛，题目也从过去玩具一样的 CTF 题目到如今极其复杂的多阶段渗透题目。随着基模能力的提升，渗透智能体的能力也越来越超乎大家的想象，放去年，如果某个厂商说自家的渗透智能体打护网能第一，可能大家会觉得是背后的安服仔累冒烟了，但放在今年，大家会相信这确实是渗透智能体自己的能力，毕竟关于 Artex 、 Cairn 的新闻层出不穷，一个好的开源渗透智能体搭配 deepseek 就能拥有超越过去资深红队的能力，独自完成大型项目的突破。
2023：Assistant for Pentest
回顾
AI for Secuirty
的发展历史，利用 LLM 辅助进行渗透测试的想法并不稀奇，早在 cursor、claude code 这类通用 Agent 还未出现的 2023 年，8 月发布在 arXiv 上的 PentestGPT 就小小的火了一把。PentestGPT 的作者认为 LLM 已经具备一定的渗透测试知识，能够理解工具输出、提出攻击思路和生成命令，但很难在漫长的渗透过程中保持完整的上下文，比如 LLM 可能在扫描多个服务后忘记之前发现的漏洞线索，或者过度关注眼前的任务，缺乏全局规划能力，于是 PentestGPT 将渗透测试拆分成三个由独立 LLM Session 驱动的模块：
推理模块
：负责整体攻击规划。利用 Pentesting Task Tree（PTT）记录已发现的信息、任务进度与候选攻击路径，并决定下一步应该做什么。
生成模块
：负责具体操作。将推理模块选定的任务转化为可执行的渗透测试命令，例如 Nmap 扫描命令。
解析模块
：负责处理工具输出、HTTP 响应和源代码等信息，提取关键内容，避免大量冗余文本占用上下文。
三个模块彼此之间形成一个循环：
Reasoning(根据 PTT 选择下一步渗透任务)->Generation(生成具体的工具命令和操作步骤)->人工执行测试命令(获得目标环境的真实反馈)->Parsing(提取执行结果中的关键信息，反馈给 Reasoning 更新 PTT)->进入下一轮
当然，敏锐的师傅已经发现了，怎么这个渗透智能体也不智能啊，为什么还得人工执行命令？这就要说到当时 2023 年的业界风潮了，当时的主流 Agent 思想是利用 workflow 把流程写死，让路径先于执行确定，节点负责局部工作，路径和传递关系由人预先设计，Dify 也就是在那时候火起来的。由于人们需要可控性，并不那么信任将一切都交给 LLM 自主完成，所以这种系统本质上还只是Human-in-the-Loop 的半自动系统。和如今人负责意图指定，AI 负责执行的路子相反，当时的主流的思想还是 AI 负责规划、生成命令与分析反馈，具体命令仍由人类执行，再将结果反馈给系统，所以 PentestGPT 其实还称不上是真正的渗透智能体，而只是一个能够规划攻击步骤、分析执行结果的智能渗透助手。
2024：Subtask for Pentest
随着 LLM 和 Agent 的发展，人们愈发意识到 PentestGPT 所代表的路线并不是真正的渗透智能体，我们想要的不是让 LLM 辅助渗透测试，而是需要让 LLM 自主完成从信息收集、漏洞分析到漏洞利用的完整流程，于是一年后的 arxiv 上出现了一篇名为 PentestAgent 的论文。从论文名字上也能看出差别，PentestGPT 只是 GPT，还只是一个 ChatBox，而 PentestAgent 代表了更大的野心，他们想要的不只是一个对话机器人，而是一个能独立完成完整渗透任务的智能体。
这时以 PentestAgent 为代表的 Agent 将渗透拆分成不同的子任务，用不同的子 Agent 来负责不同的环节：
信息收集
：自主执行 Nmap 等工具，根据执行结果迭代扫描，识别目标服务及版本，并记录环境信息。
知识检索
：根据发现的服务和版本，搜索漏洞数据库、GitHub、ExploitDB 等资源，收集相关 CVE、PoC 和利用教程。
攻击规划
：借助 RAG，从检索结果中先筛选潜在攻击面，再选择具体的漏洞利用方案。
攻击执行
：根据 PoC 和目标环境准备参数、执行利用，并通过 Self-reflection 分析执行错误、修改命令或代码后重试。
这时由于 RAG 技术的流行，以及模型厂商并没有把重点放在 cyber 模型上，原始的模型虽然训练了一部分网安数据，但在网安任务上的表现仍没有那么智能，于是利用 RAG 为模型补充所缺少的安全知识成为了常态，以 PentestGPT 为例，PentestGPT 将知识分为两个层次：
Coarse-grained Knowledge
：哪些软件版本可能存在什么漏洞。
Procedure-level Knowledge
：这些漏洞具体应该如何利用，包括 PoC 和执行条件。
此时的渗透智能体虽然终于能够摆脱人工干预了，但还是有一个很大的缺点，与其说它是渗透智能体，不如说它是一个 CVE 复现智能体，其主要工作方式其实只是识别目标软件、检索已知漏洞、找到现成 PoC，再尝试执行。因此，PentestAgent 虽然能够自动完成许多已知漏洞的利用任务，却不代表它具备很强的未知漏洞发现能力。作者自己也在论文中坦率的提到，复杂的多漏洞组合与攻击链规划不在其主要研究范围内。
2025：Pentest for CTF
到了 2025 年年底，腾讯举办了第一届 AI 渗透大赛，国内涌现出了许多优秀的渗透智能体，但值得注意的是，此时比赛的题目仍然只是 CTF 题目 Xbow，所以此时的经验其实并不一定能直接复用到真实环境中。当我们听第一届比赛的战队的答辩时，也能看出来他们大部分是继承了 PentestGPT 的思想，将完整的渗透任务拆分成不同的子任务交给不同的子 Agent 完成，给 LLM 提供专家经验，对渗透场景进行特定的建模，且越来越多的系统开始直接利用通用 Agent 架构：
Plan-and-Execute
：先将渗透目标拆解成多个子任务，再逐步执行。
ReAct
：在每个子任务内部不断进行推理、工具调用、观察反馈和调整。
MCP + Sandbox
：通过统一接口调用终端、浏览器等工具，在隔离环境中自主进行渗透测试
比如涙笑师傅将这种建模称作”意图工程”，他认为人类渗透测试专家并不是毫无章法地探索，而是针对不同环境有不同的测试策略。例如，测试办公网网站时，可能先判断认证机制，再根据认证结果选择后续测试方向，于是他希望把安全专家的渗透经验从代码和 Prompt 中抽离出来，变成可复用、可组合的执行流程，把安全专家经验显式建模，他将这样的结构称作 Agent Pattern Graph（APG），使用 YAML 定义有向图：
节点表示高层测试任务、预期输出。
边表示根据执行结果选择的下一步。
Runtime 负责解释执行，由 Agent 完成节点中的具体任务。
另一个变化在于，过去大家尝试用 MCP 之类的方式给 LLM 提供 tool，但对着基模能力的提升，其实完全不必再让 LLM 逐个调用工具，而是让 LLM 编写 Python 代码，由代码批量编排工具调用、处理结果，最后只把关键信息返回给模型，这个设计同时减少了 LLM 调用次数和无关中间信息进入上下文的问题
2026：Pentest for Realworld
随着第二届腾讯 AI 渗透大赛的举办，渗透智能体的架构终于又迎来了新的颠覆性的改变。无论是 24 年还是 25 年，大家都是预定义 Recon、Planning、Execution 等角色，或者安排固定的攻击流程，但涙笑师傅认为不应预先规定 Agent 应当如何渗透，而是让多个 Agent 基于共享事实，自主探索通往目标的路径，渗透测试本质上只有三个要素：
Origin（起点）
：已知的目标及初始环境。
Goal（终点）
：明确的任务完成条件，例如获取 Flag。
Path（路径）
：未知，需要 Agent 自主探索。
因此，Cairn 不预定义角色、不预定义工作流，也不强制遵循某套渗透测试方法论，而是围绕目标持续搜索，核心是一个共享黑板，所有 Agent 都围绕黑板工作，黑板维护三类信息：
Fact
：已确认的事实，例如发现某个服务或成功验证某个漏洞
Intent
：下一步准备探索的方向，例如尝试某种攻击路径
Hint
：人类提供的提示或额外判断
这些信息逐渐形成一张从 Origin 向 Goal 生长的 Fact–Intent Graph，多个平等的 Worker 通过共享黑板间接协作，不需要互相发送消息，也没有固定的“扫描专家”“漏洞专家”等角色，这种协作方式被作者称为
Stigmergy
，类似蚁群通过共享环境留下的信息协调行动，系统只有三种任务类型：
Bootstrap
：首先尝试直接完成 Goal
Reason
：读取现有 Fact，判断目标是否完成，生成新的 Intent
Explore
：Worker 领取 Intent，执行探索并写入新的 Fact
更新共享黑板，继续 Reason / Explore
每个 Worker 内部遵循 OODA 循环（Observe、Orient、Decide、Act），调度器负责分配任务并管理 Worker 的运行环境，而具体的探索过程交给 Worker 自己决定。架构能有这样的颠覆性改变，当然也离不开基模本身的发展，随着模型自身能力越来越强，过去我们加在 Agent 上的引导终于变成了约束，Simple is better，让 LLM 自由发挥反而能发挥出更强大的能力
黑板架构和 2025 年的 APG 在设计哲学上几乎走向了两个相反的方向，APG 认为通用 Agent 缺乏专家经验，应当通过结构化流程约束它的行为；Cairn 则认为预定义流程和角色可能限制模型的探索能力，应该让工作流从执行过程中自然形成。这并不能证明 Cairn 的设计普遍优于 APG，但说明随着基础模型和通用 Agent 能力增强，研究者开始重新思考：究竟应该给 Agent 增加多少领域知识和人工约束？
Now
虽然 2026 年尚未过去，但基于黑板架构，已然有许多优秀的渗透智能体出现，比如登上 FBI 、被许多 APT 团队使用的 Artex，虽然它也采用了黑板架构中 Fact、Intent、Hint 的这一套东西，但它其实本质上和 Cairn 有非常大的差别。Artex 通过双图架构维护长期探索状态，通过集中式 Planner 协调多个 Worker，并引入事件驱动机制持续推进攻击链，Artex 有两个图，一个是全局资产图 Asset Graph，保存了 Domain / IP / Service / Endpoint；另一个是任务探索图 Exploration Graph，保存了 Goal / Intent / Fact / Finding
两张图通过资产锚点关联，让 Agent 不仅知道我发现了什么，还知道我针对哪个资产进行了哪些尝试，相比仅依赖对话历史，这种结构化状态管理更适合持续运行的多 Agent 系统，也让 Artex 极为擅长真实环境中的 end2end 渗透利用，我在第一次使用 Artex 的时候也被小小的震撼住了，Artex 的成熟度已经到了商业产品的程度，如果他是一个收费工具，我想我会很愿意为这个工具付费。
但在任务执行这里，Artex 没有像 Cairn 一样选择让 LLM 自由的探索和发挥，而是回到了大家长式的架构，由一个 Planner 统一负责全局规划，它的工作机制是：
资产图或探索图发生变化，触发 Planner。
Planner 读取当前的资产、事实、探索进度及目标。
根据这些信息生成新的 Intent。
多个 Worker 并行领取 Intent，调用真实工具完成测试。
Worker 将结果写回图中，再次触发 Planner。
这里有两个细节：
第一，Planner 集中负责自动生成 Intent。
Worker 主要负责执行被分配的任务，从而避免多个 Worker 各自规划导致任务重复或方向冲突；
第二，Planner 并不是每次都必须生成任务。
如果当前没有值得继续探索的方向，可以不派发新的 Intent，避免无意义的重复测试。所以本质上，它采用的是集中式全局决策 + 并行局部探索的架构，相比于弱化中心化规划，让探索路径从 Worker 的协作中自然产生的 Cairn，Artex 的设计牺牲了自由度，但却在真实渗透场景中更稳定。
我们也能想象到作者采用这样的设计的原因，多 Agent 协同工作的一个最大的痛点就是并发和竞争，worker A 可能会不小心删除掉 worker B 创建的账号，worker C 也可能一不小心打崩 worker B 正在测试的服务，而通过集中的意图下发能极大的减少掉这样的问题；另一方面，集中的意图管理也更加可控，可以通过监督主 planner 的行为来防止 Agent 产生过激的行为(e.g., 虽然即便如此我们也能时不时听说某小白用 Artex 把网站打崩了的新闻)，而 Artex 为了真实环境的可靠和稳定其实也已经做出了不少的努力，比如有流量监控，也有默认的命令黑名单。
当然了，Artex 也不是完美的，我想也有不少师傅尝试用二开的 Artex 打 tsecbench 或者一些渗透智能体的比赛，但至少从我自己的测试结果来看，效果并不是那么的理想。老话说的好，渗透测试的本质是信息搜集，做渗透 Agent 的本质其实是做 Agent team，核心是如何让 Agent 之间更好的交流，比如黑板架构是通过一块黑板让所有 worker 共享信息并产出事实和意图，每个 worker 拿到一个意图进行工作，然后产出事实和下一步的意图，但 Artex 其实是没有 Agent 之间的信息交流的，它是大家长式的架构，worker 只负责工作，策略和调度都由中央 Planner 决定，所以可想而知，其实有很多宝贵的信息都在这个过程中遗失了
另一个严重的问题我把它称作意图偏移，Artex 中唯一的信息交流窗口就是 worker 和 planner 之间，worker 给 planner 生成 fact，planner 给 worker 下发 intent，很显然，这个过程之间是有信息损失的，特别是，worker 可能会错误理解 intent，最后反馈给 planner 错误的 fact，而这个过程越长意图越可能偏移，这里以一个我用 Artex 打 tsecbench v1 的例子为例，这里 planner 给 worker 下发的任务是
“其中/sql/与/common/值得进一步探文件”
：
但 worker 对于这个 intent 的理解竟然变成了
“fact83显示仅剩/sql/、/common/两个真实目录可深挖”
:
于是，当 worker 将这两个目录测试完发现无法进一步利用之后，反馈给 planner 的 fact 变成了
“路径遍历不可行，因为路径都测试完了”
，planner 也就这样基于错误的事实进行下一步的规划，认为这条路子走不通，而事实上目录遍历是可行的，只是不是这两个目录罢了，得试试其他的路径。这就是大家长式的集中规划在长路径渗透场景中最大的问题——错误的 fact 会传播，一个 worker 的结论被当作最终结论，而随着渗透路径越来越长，这样的意图偏移会越来越容易发生。毕竟在这个架构中，唯一的信息交流途径就是 intent 和 fact，而交流是基于信任的，而这样的信任有时候并没有那么可靠。
My design
我当时打第三届腾讯渗透 AI 大赛其实就是基于的 Artex，但后来发现这样的架构其实并不那么适合这类刷榜型的比赛，Artex 强调的其实是安全可靠的在真实场景完成渗透任务，而并没有发挥出 LLM 真正的能力。于是我后面并没有基于 Artex 的老路子，而是自己换了一种新的架构，在 tsecbench v2 和 bctf 的排行榜上也终于打进前十了
这里我也分享一下我自己的感悟，当然，这些感悟也只针对于 tsecbench 这类刷榜型的比赛，和真实渗透场景无关，我也没有拿真实环境测过。我们知道渗透测试的本质是信息搜集，再进一步，其实渗透的本质是一种
trial and error
的过程，反复试错，靠尝试摸索。就像陶哲轩描述自己解数学难题的过程一样——不同于刻板印象中大家认为解数学难题主要靠的是某一个瞬间的灵光一现，实际的过程往往是测试一种方法发现行不通，于是尝试另一种方法，经过不断的失败和尝试终于让答案变得清晰，最后找到答案的时候甚至会懊恼自己真傻，为什么之前没发现。
真实的渗透测试往往也是这样，靠的是耐心和专注，通过一次一次的失败与测试终于找到突破口最后利用成功。反映在 Agent 上的一个有趣的现象是，低思考模式的 Agent 效果反而更好，比如我拿自己的 Agent 做过一次对比实验，将 Worker 的思考模式配置成 low、high、max 的分数反而不如把三个 Worker 全都配成 low 的分数好，翻了一下日志我发现这个有趣的现象的成因在于，高思考程度的 LLM 往往会三思而后行，先在脑海里提出各种假设然后否决各种假设，最后选出一个看起来最行之有效的方法，而对于低思考程度的 LLM 反而会不管三七二十一，先试了再说，特别是 BCTF 里”墨记轻博客”这题，出题人应该是额外做了一些针对 LLM 的误导，会让 LLM 以为这个 SSTI 引擎是 JS 的，但实际上是 Java 的，于是 Agent 会反复用 JS 的 SSTI 语法做测试，最后一次又一次的碰壁，认为这道题无解。但对于低思考程度的模型，它反而不会想这么多，会先把所有常见的引擎特征都试一遍，反而不会掉入陷阱，能发现这个引擎到底是什么。
另一个针对这类刷榜的比赛的经验就是，设计一个好的调度的算法确实是很有必要的。比如第三届腾讯 AI 渗透比赛里其实有很多多 flag 的题，众所周知，多 flag 的题和单 flag 题的权重当然不是一样的，多 flag 题肯定需要更多的时间才能做出来，但我当时没意识到这个问题，导致一些其实能拿分的多 flag 题也没时间做了。后来赛后从我自己的体验来看，最有效的方法其实还是用时间片算法，比如靶场里是同时能开三个题目，就建议两个 lane 去做单 flag 题，一个 lane 去做多 flag 题，单 flag 题的时间片可以短一点，比如 30 分钟，到点就换下一道题，多 flag 题的时间片可以长一点，比如 45 分钟，这样可以防止无休止的把时间浪费在一些做不出来的题上，有更多的时间去做那些能拿分的题。
最后一个经验就是让 LLM 多做做反思，因为 LLM 其实很容易走进死胡同，忽略了那些重要的细节，甚至最后放空大脑，在后台挂一个一个小时的超级并发爆破进程。从我自己的感觉来看，如果一个题目第一个 pass 的三十分钟里 Agent 没做出来这题，那就说明 LLM 可能走进死胡同或者有什么关键的细节没有注意到，所以每个题的的第二次重做的 pass 里，我会在开头继承之前的进度以及中间 15 分钟的时候都触发一次反思，让它思考自己过去有没有没有尝试的思路、忽略的细节或者错误的假设。关键就是让 LLM 批判性的审视过去的进展，因为可能之前的 LLM 建立在了错误的假设之上，忽略了关键的细节，比如 BCTF “墨记轻博客”这题 LLM 可能会一直以为这题是 JS 的引擎，”ColdByte 冷论坛” 这题会一直认为这个模板引擎没有执行命令，最后结合了几篇 AI 会上的论文：
Reflexion (NeurIPS 2023)：回顾过去的失败，改变策略，吸取教训
Self-Refine (NeurIPS 2023)：批判先前的输出，迭代改进
Chain-of-Verification (ACL 2024)：主动寻找需要验证的假设与事实
SELF-DISCOVER (NeurIPS 2024)：重新组织解决问题的思维框架
CRITIC (ICLR 2024)：利用工具和外部反馈纠正自身错误
我给 LLM 喂的反思提示词最后是：
Conduct a critical retrospective of your work so far. Do not simply summarize your progress or defend your previous decisions.
Examine the task, available evidence, previous actions, observations, and failures. In particular:
1. Unchallenged assumptions: What have you treated as true without sufficient verification? Which conclusions depend on these assumptions?
2. Overlooked details: What clues, anomalies, errors, or seemingly insignificant observations did you fail to investigate?
3. Unexplored possibilities: Which promising approaches have you not attempted? Did you prematurely dismiss any option because it appeared difficult, unlikely, unconventional, or inconsistent with your initial hypothesis?
4. Strategic mistakes: Have you been repeating similar actions, optimizing a flawed approach, or becoming anchored to your earlier conclusions?
5. Alternative explanations: What fundamentally different hypotheses could explain the available evidence? What observations would distinguish them?
6. Next experiments: Identify the most informative, feasible tests that could challenge your current understanding or unlock new progress.
Distinguish confirmed facts from hypotheses. Do not invent previous attempts or assume something failed without evidence. Prioritize genuinely new, testable directions over superficial variations of strategies already tried.
Conclude with a revised action plan, and execute the highest-priority feasible next step if tools and permissions allow.
聊完宏观上的感悟，最后来聊聊我自己的设计，后期在 Artex 的基础上改代码的时候愈发觉得 Artex 的 harness 其实很大程度上限制了 LLM 的主观能动性。它可能能非常合格的完成一些人工指定的任务，能熟练的应用一些常见的技术和思路完成目标，但到了需要发散思路，解决一些难题的时候，这样的 harness 反而成了束缚他最大的枷锁。
现在的基模比如 deepseek 的能力其实已经很强了，哪怕只是 codex 接 deepseek 其实也已经能完成许多渗透任务了，所以现在的核心不是引导 LLM ，而是给他足够的空间和时间发挥自己的能力，让不同的 Agent 协作配合，共同完成任务。比如最近微软的一篇
论文
其实也采用了和 Cairn 非常类似的架构，子 Agent 之间不区分角色，而是合作完成任务，通过行之有效的信息交流，甚至能实现 1024 个 Agent 一起协同工作，而随着 Agent 数量的提升，彼此之间竟然没有产生干扰，而是把任务完成的越来越好，就像 openai 用 10,000 个并发 AI Agent 协同工作攻破 NS 方程一样。
最后我自己的设计是对于一个给定的任务三个 worker 协同工作，底座 Agent 是 PI。无论是 Cairn 的黑板，还是 Artex 的中央 Planner，解决的其实都是 Agent 之间彼此交流的问题。Agent 需要彼此交流才能取长补短，测试不同的思路，得到不同的信息，但这里我并不认可像 Artex 一样由某个 Planner 集中下发思路，很简单，因为这种做法只能基于 worker 给出的 fact 做出判断，而对于一些复杂的情况，worker 在测试的时候不一定能意识到自己遇到了某个关键信息并把它写进 fact，而是很有可能将它忽略，相反，由 worker 自己做决策就少了这样一层的信息交流的损失，反而有可能注意到这些宝贵的小细节。
最后我的设计可能比黑板还要简单一点，毕竟黑板其实也是有 fact、intent、finding 的，某种程度上也算是一种对 LLM 的约束，最后我只是提供了一个可以让 Worker 之间做交流的公共黑板——LLM 可以自由选择向这个公共的黑板写入什么，也可以主动向不同的其他 worker 发信息，比如提醒它某个工作它已经在做了不要再尝试或者不要做破坏性的行为，每个 worker 在执行工具之前也会主动查看一下黑板上的信息或者其他 worker 发过来的信息。
这样的设计的核心就是减少对 LLM 的约束，只向 LLM 提供额外的信息，而不约束已有的能力，希望能尽量发挥出 LLM 自己的能力，就像微软的 Agensh 其实也并没有显式的 intent，每个 Agent 开始工作前，只是先查看共同目标、现有代码和其他成员的进度，找出尚未完成的部分，再在共享看板上发布认领声明，说明自己准备负责什么，如果彼此之间出现冲突则直接发消息协商，调整各自的工作范围。从我分析日志的结果来看，大部分时候共享黑板上写入的都是每个 worker 自己的 finding 以及自己打算做什么，如果某些 finding 极其有价值，worker 也会主动向那个 worker 发消息请求更多的信息。当然，这样的缺点就是实在太自由了，很多时候会出现并发竞争的问题，比如某个 worker 在做爆破，可能就会影响到另一个 worker 手上的活，不过这时候 worker 之间也会主动发信息做协商，提醒它别爆破了，所以这样过于自由的架构也会带来风险，就像一群住在同一个工位、可以随时互相推翻结论的疯子，它可能能做到一些别人做不了的事，也可能让事情变得更糟。不过从我自己的感受来看，这样的工作效率是比类似 Artex 的集中意图下发要好的多，也更容易做出来之前做不出来的难题，比如强网杯的时候这道 ezcms 我的 Agent 用了不到 20 分钟就拿到一血了，我印象里二血的耗时至少比我多一倍：

items.content:
This article was co-posted on the Horizon Offensive Security Team (HOST) blog
here
.
When we find ourselves in the position of being able to compromise a number of employee workstations during a red team engagement, we tend to target IT staff and sysadmins specifically, gaining persistent access to their work laptops through C2 implants. In some cases, we run surveillance on their machines for days or weeks, waiting for them to open password managers, authenticate to internal services, and access infrastructure we can’t reach directly.
Among the dumped cookies and backdoored KeePass databases, we regularly come across IT people using
mRemoteNG
to manage remote connections.
Their vault files are often protected with non-default passwords and offline cracking doesn’t always get us in; that said, we can dump the memory of an already running and decrypted vault and - as it turns out - that’s all you need.
Using the technique described in this post, we’ve been able to gain privileged access to entire client infrastructures on more than one occasion.
What’s mRemoteNG?
mRemoteNG
is an open-source connection manager for Windows that lets users save credentials for several protocols like SSH, RDP and many others. All testing in this post was performed against
mRemoteNG v1.76.20
(the latest stable release at the time of writing).
This is what a newly-created mRemoteNG vault looks like.
Details about saved connections are stored in an XML file located at
C:\Users\<USERNAME>\AppData\Roaming\mRemoteNG\confCons.xml
by default; this file contains all the information used by the software to decrypt the vault at runtime.
When a vault is protected with a custom password, opening the configuration file as a new vault prompts for the password, so getting access to the file alone isn’t enough.

This means that mRemoteNG uses a default password to avoid storing cleartext credentials in the configuration file; this is not a new discovery and there are several PoCs and scripts that aim to decrypt vault credentials either with the default password of

Using a PoC like
this one
we can parse the configuration file and decrypt the passwords by using the default password.
For the usernames and hostnames in the configuration file to be encrypted as well, the
FullFileEncryption
field needs to be set to
true
.
This value is
false
by default, but enabling it prevents an attacker who obtains the configuration file from seeing which users and hosts the vault owner connects to.
Attacking hardened vault configurations
By setting
Password protect
to
yes
, a user can change the default password to a (hopefully) more secure one.
The change is reflected in the configuration file: you’ll see the
Protected
attribute change and all the passwords be encrypted to new base64 blobs. This also means that running the same PoC as before will no longer be able to decrypt the passwords from the configuration file.
Of course any password can still be subjected to offline bruteforce attacks, but
what if the password is complex and cracking it is not an option
?
Accessing plaintext credentials from within mRemoteNG
Once a password has been saved in the vault, mRemoteNG does not allow a user to view it in plaintext.
A fairly old workaround is to use the “External Tools” feature, the method is described
here
and consists in opening a
cmd
window and printing the
%password%
environment variable to screen, effectively revealing the password stored for a specific vault entry.
This technique is useless for our situation since you need interactive access to the vault to set it up, but it tells us something important about how the program works: all the encrypted passwords are loaded from the configuration file and decrypted at runtime.
This leaves two possible attack paths:
Spin up a hidden VNC server and use it along with the C2 session on the laptop to interact with the user’s desktop and perform the “External Tools” trick to reveal the plaintext passwords stored in the vault
Perform a complete memory dump of the mRemoteNG process, download it locally and extract the decrypted credentials from there
The first method is too invasive for most situations since it requires interacting with the application on the user’s desktop (not on a hidden one) without getting noticed. The second only needs an implant running with enough privileges to read the process memory.
Dumping mRemoteNG’s memory
The idea of dumping mRemoteNG’s memory to extract credentials is not new.
CVE-2023-30367
documents that mRemoteNG loads configuration files into memory in plaintext at startup, and a
public PoC
exists that searches the dump for the raw XML config data.
The recommended mitigation for that CVE is to use a strong encryption password on the vault but that doesn’t really hold up. The CVE PoC recovers the
decrypted config
from memory, which is only useful when the vault uses the default
mR3m
key (something you could already get by just reading
confCons.xml
off disk).
Our approach is different: we extract the
master key itself
from the process memory, then use it to decrypt the configuration file offline; this approach is better overall as it works regardless of password complexity.
With an implant running as
NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
or as the target user, performing a memory dump of the process is trivial and it’s only a matter of doing it without being detected by the EDR installed on the system. We typically use a custom .NET assembly that can be loaded into memory to dump a target process and place the encrypted contents on disk for download and offline decryption.
The tool itself doesn’t do anything special: it suspends the process’ memory before dumping and resumes it afterwards to avoid running into problems given by changes made in program memory during the dump which would result in a corrupted and structurally inconsistent dump file. The whole suspend-dump-resume cycle completes in under a second, so the user is unlikely to notice.
Before doing any research one this, we did not know whether the decryption key (the initial password) was stored in memory even after the initial decryption process; after all, mRemoteNG only seems to decrypt credentials once so we only knew that we would find those passwords and had no certainty of finding the master key.
The password-protected vault we used to test memory extraction techniques shown in the previous section was protected with the password
Host11!
so one thing we can do to figure out whether the decryption key is stored in memory is to perform a memory dump of our own process and just look for the UTF-16 LE string.
Both the master key (
Host11!
) and the decrypted entry password (
SomethingSecure123!
) are visible in the dump:
Further tests showed that the number of occurrences of the master key in memory varies but there should always be
at least one
.
Tracing the memory layout
To automate extraction we needed a reliable byte pattern to locate the master key programmatically so we opened the dump in a hex editor and looked at the bytes surrounding the
Host11!
string and found a sequence of contiguous .NET
System.String

Fortunately, the password manager is open source so we can trace each of these strings back to the mRemoteNG source code starting with

"Password:"
,
"Verify:"

"Password"

The master key
"Host11!"
comes from the
txtPassword
TextBox where the user types their password to decrypt the vault at runtime. When the form closes, the code converts it to a
SecureString
and clears the TextBox:

Setting

creates a new empty string, but the original
"Host11!"

Since .NET strings are immutable reference types, clearing the TextBox just drops the reference without zeroing the memory, causing the string to persist until the garbage collector reclaims it, and even then the bytes may linger in the memory page.
The strings after the master key (
"Type"
,
"connection"
,
"Expanded"
,
"Id"
,
"Descr"
, …) are XML attribute names allocated during deserialization of

The reason all these strings end up adjacent on the heap is straightforward: the .NET managed heap allocates objects sequentially from an allocation pointer.
The password form initialization, user input, and config file parsing all happen in quick succession during startup, so their string allocations land in order on the heap.
Here is what the

As covered in the walkthrough above, the script encodes the
"Password:"
signature as a 17-byte partial UTF-16 LE sequence and skips the 15-byte .NET string object overhead to land directly on the next string’s character data.
To make this more stable and flexible, if the byte at the start of the candidate region is not null, it reads forward until a UTF-16 LE null terminator and treats whatever printable string it finds as a master key candidate.
The image below shows the script finding several candidates, including the actual vault key (
Host11!
).
We then integrated this logic with the decryption code from
mremoteng_decrypt.py
into a second script that finds master key candidates and tries each one against the encrypted passwords in the configuration file. If a candidate successfully decrypts an entry, it stops and prints the result.
The full source code for both scripts is available in our
GitHub repository
.
Backup plan
The pattern we found and used in both scripts to extract master key candidates is pretty specific, but we found that it hasn’t changed in the past year or so. If this pattern ever was to change, the method would no longer work or there might be edge-cases that we have not run into while testing.
If the scripts we provided turn out to be ineffective, it should be trivial to perform the same steps we used and find a new valid pattern; another less elegant solution is just to run
strings
on the dump, we still know both the master key and decrypted passwords are in memory so the same result could be achieved by extracting all valid UTF-16 LE strings from the binary and execute the PoC script to try every single one.
Protecting against this attack
Privileges required
The examples in this post show the memory dump being performed from an implant running as
NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
, but that’s more privilege than strictly necessary.
Any user can read the virtual memory of processes running in their own security context so no special privilege is needed. If an attacker has a shell as the target user, they can dump mRemoteNG without any privilege escalation.
For dumping processes that belong to
other
users,
SeDebugPrivilege
is required. This privilege is assigned to local administrators and the SYSTEM account by default, but it has to be explicitly enabled in the caller’s token before it takes effect.
Hardening the configuration doesn’t help
As demonstrated above, the master key lives in process memory regardless of its complexity so a strong password protects against offline config file decryption, but not against memory extraction; this was the recommended mitigation for CVE-2023-30367 and it is insufficient.
Finally,
FullFileEncryption
encrypts usernames and hostnames in the config file, but has no effect on what’s stored in process memory at runtime. The master key and decrypted credentials are present either way.
What might actually help
If mRemoteNG is the password manager of choice within your company’s technical team, creating custom detection rules to spot the “suspend, dump, resume” pattern used to dump the process’ memory. That said, this pattern can easily be changed, making the custom rules useless.
The only thing that meaningfully reduces the exposure window is using a robust password and closing mRemoteNG when you’re not using it to prevent the master key and all decrypted credentials from being accessible.
This is not a problem unique to mRemoteNG. Any application that decrypts secrets into process memory and holds them there indefinitely has the same issue. The difference is just how easy it is to find them in the dump.
What’s next for mRemoteNG
We reached out to the current maintainer of mRemoteNG before publishing this post.
The latest stable release (v1.76.20) dates back to 2019 and is no longer actively maintained and a new version is in development under a new maintainer and is expected to release in the near future.
According to the maintainer, the new version will address the issues described in this post directly, by only storing references to credential sources and pulling them on demand rather than keeping decrypted passwords in the process memory. The new version will also introduce user profiles (local and AD-backed), connection profiles that can aggregate connections from multiple sources, and RBAC for credential access.
If you or your organization use mRemoteNG, the nightly build (v1.78.2) is already available on the project’s GitHub and we suggest keeping an eye out for any new updates coming in the future.

AI Infrastructure Keeps Getting Attacked — NEAR AI’s SGLang Breach Is Just the Latest Warning
NEAR AI’s SGLang breach is the latest example that AI infrastructure continues to be a focus for malicious actors—and Langflow’s string of critical CVEs provide an additional proof point. Learn why continuous exposure validation, not another patch cycle, is the fix.
Summary
Latest breach:
NEAR AI disclosed on November 9, 2026 that an attacker had exploited a vulnerability in SGLang—an open-source inference engine—exposing account details for roughly 100 users and chat histories from 18 legacy AI agents outside its confidential-computing environment. It’s the latest reminder that AI infrastructure is where attackers are focused.
Proof point:
Langflow, a widely used open-source platform for building AI agents and RAG pipelines, has racked up at least seven critical CVEs since mid-2025, with five landing on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog—the clearest example yet of the pattern.
Attackers aren’t waiting:
Langflow’s CVE-2026-33017 (March) was weaponized within 20 hours of disclosure, leaving little time for defenders to take action.
Credential magnet:
The payoff isn’t just a compromised server—it’s the credentials AI infrastructure stores by design: LLM provider keys, cloud credentials, and database passwords.
Coverage gap:
Most exposure management programs still don’t test AI agent and pipeline infrastructure the way they test networks and endpoints, and attackers have already found that gap.
The fix:
Security leaders must evolve their security processes to fold AI infrastructure into a continuous
adversarial exposure validation (AEV)
program—proving whether these systems can actually be exploited in their environment, before someone else does.
Author:
Koby Bar, Senior Vice President of Product
On November 9, 2026,
NEAR AI disclosed that an attacker had exploited a vulnerability in SGLang
, an open-source LLM inference engine, exposing account details—including names and email addresses—for roughly 100 users, and chat histories, settings, and logs from 18 legacy AI agents that weren’t running in its confidential-computing environment.
It’s the latest reminder that AI infrastructure is where attackers are now focusing.
Langflow
, a widely used open-source platform for building AI agents and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, has served as a similar proof point over the last year. It has racked up at least seven critical CVEs since mid-2025, including
CVE-2026-33017
, which was disclosed in March 2026 as an unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaw in a public Langflow endpoint that was unauthenticated by design. It was weaponized within 20 hours of public disclosure—before a proof-of-concept exploit was even circulating publicly, according to researchers at
Sysdig
.
Both SGLang and Langflow are examples of the kinds of platforms and tools that have quickly appeared inside enterprise environments as teams race to stand up AI capabilities. Together, they highlight the same risk pattern: security programs haven’t caught up to how fast AI infrastructure is being deployed.
Why AI Infrastructure Keeps Getting Attacked
It’s tempting to read NEAR AI’s SGLang breach as an isolated incident, or Langflow’s CVE count as a Langflow-specific problem. But it’s more useful to read both as previews of what security leaders can expect to keep happening across AI infrastructure broadly, and a guide to how security programs need to evolve to combat this new reality.
Inference servers like SGLang sit on some of the most sensitive assets in an AI stack: API keys, live request data, and session context. That concentration of risk is exactly what played out at NEAR AI—two customers had API keys exposed in server logs, and the attacker could see live requests being processed on the compromised server.
Agent-orchestration platforms like Langflow carry a similar concentration of risk. Langflow’s Global Variables store is designed to hold things like model API keys, cloud credentials, and database passwords, all in one place so AI workflows can run smoothly. While that is a sensible design for an AI orchestration tool, it also creates the kind of concentrated, high-value target that security teams historically haven’t had on their radar because it didn’t exist in their environment two years ago.
Enterprises are standing up AI agents, RAG pipelines, and
model context protocol (MCP)-based tooling
faster than security programs are extending coverage to support them. Most vulnerability scanning, patch cadences, and exposure management programs were built around networks, endpoints, cloud workloads, and identity—not around the orchestration layer that now sits between your data and a model that can act on it.
Attackers aren’t waiting for security teams to catch up.
IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report
found that AI-enabled breaches now average $6 million, roughly $1 million above the global average, and that more than one in five organizations have already had a breach targeting their own AI models or applications. Governments are sounding the same alarm: a June 2026
joint statement from the Five Eyes cyber agencies
warned boards and executives directly that “AI is shortening the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation,” and that “cyber risk assumptions can become outdated in months, not years.”
The Question Isn’t Whether You’re Patched. It’s Whether You’re Exposed.
Patch compliance and real-world exploitability are not the same thing—and that gap is where most AI infrastructure risk actually lives. For example, confirming that Langflow is on the latest version tells you a vulnerability has been remediated. It doesn’t tell you whether your specific deployment—your Global Variables configuration, your network exposure, your guardrails, your connected credentials—was ever actually reachable by the techniques attackers used against CVE-2026-33017. It also doesn’t tell you what else is exposed right now that hasn’t made it into a CVE yet.
NEAR AI’s own breach report makes a related point. Its confidential-computing hardware worked exactly as designed, protecting data from the operator and the host. What it didn’t do—because it isn’t built to—was protect against a vulnerability in the software running inside that environment, and that’s exactly where the attacker got in. The control held up; the assumption about what it covered didn’t, and nobody had tested that assumption against a real attack. Having a control in place isn’t the same as knowing it will hold during an actual incident.
That’s exactly what
adversarial exposure validation (AEV)
is built to answer—and why AI infrastructure belongs inside a
continuous threat exposure management (CTEM)
program rather than a one-off “AI security” initiative. CTEM is built on the premise that your exposure changes constantly—new deployments, new configurations, new attacker techniques—and that the only way to keep pace is to validate continuously, not to scan on a quarterly schedule and hope nothing changes in between. NEAR AI’s SGLang breach and Langflow’s CVE count are both textbook cases for why that premise holds.
AI Infrastructure Exposure Validation: Testing the Way Attackers Do
Most security programs are not yet testing AI infrastructure with the same attacker-eye-view rigor applied to everything else in their environment.
SafeBreach AI Security Validation
is content within the SafeBreach CTEM Platform that safely simulates real-world attacks against an organization’s AI applications and AI infrastructure to prove whether its defenses stop them. Simulations are run against your production model with your guardrails, system instructions, and knowledge base in place, and each returns a clear Blocked or Not Blocked verdict and remediation guidance.
Results map to frameworks security teams already report against, including the
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
, the
OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications
, and
MITRE ATLAS
.
SafeBreach AI Security Validation covers four critical areas:
Guardrails Validation:
Tests whether AI guardrails stop data leakage, system prompt leakage, harmful content generation, and malicious code generation. Supports models on Amazon Bedrock and Azure OpenAI.
AI Infrastructure Testing:
Tests whether attackers can exploit known vulnerabilities in AI orchestration software.
Shadow AI Validation:
Tests whether data loss prevention (DLP) controls stop employees from sharing sensitive data with public AI chatbots.
Custom AI Attacks:
Lets teams build their own AI attacks with the SafeBreach AI Security skill in VS Code.
This kind of continuous validation is built to keep pace with AI-driven threats. It isn’t a one-time AI risk assessment or a patch tracker. It’s ongoing proof of whether the systems holding your model keys, cloud credentials, and session data would stand up to the techniques attackers are using against AI infrastructure today.
Don’t Wait for the Next Breach to Prove the Point
AI infrastructure will continue to be the focus of malicious actors, and the underlying dynamic isn’t specific to one platform or tool. The risk is applicable to AI infrastructure broadly and is a symptom of the fact that it has been adopted faster than testing can keep up at most organizations.
Schedule a demo
to see how SafeBreach’s CTEM Platform and AI Security Validation content test AI infrastructure alongside the rest of your environment—continuously, not just when the next CVE makes headlines.
About the Author
Koby Bar
is Senior Vice President of Product at SafeBreach, where he leads the company’s product strategy and roadmap. With more than 16 years of experience in product leadership across early-stage startups and large, established organizations, Koby has a strong track record of turning complex security challenges into products customers rely on. He leads a team of product managers, designers, and technical writers focused on delivering an exceptional user experience and maximizing the value of the SafeBreach CTEM Platform. Most recently, he has driven the company’s AI strategy, including the launch of SafeBreach Helm, the LLM-driven engine that connects the pillars of CTEM, and the company’s new AI agents. Before joining SafeBreach in 2022, Koby held product leadership roles at IRONSCALES and Rogers Communications. He is a University of Toronto alumni.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is AI infrastructure exposure validation?
AI infrastructure exposure validation is the practice of testing whether the platforms running your AI agents, pipelines, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems can actually be exploited by real attack techniques, not just confirming they’re patched. It applies adversarial exposure validation (AEV) methods—simulated, safe attacks—to AI orchestration tools the same way security teams already test networks and endpoints.
Why do AI infrastructure platforms like Langflow and SGLang keep getting exploited?
The underlying dynamic is the same across AI infrastructure: enterprises adopt AI infrastructure faster than security programs build testing and monitoring around it. Agent-orchestration platforms like Langflow concentrate high-value secrets—model API keys, cloud credentials, and database passwords—in a layer most security programs haven’t extended coverage to yet; Langflow alone has had at least seven critical CVEs surface since mid-2025. Inference-serving platforms like SGLang concentrate their own high-value assets—model access and live session data—which is what made the NEAR AI breach possible. Both are symptoms of the same gap.
What’s the difference between patching an AI platform and validating it?
Patching confirms a known vulnerability has been remediated in the software version you’re running. Validation confirms whether your specific deployment—its configuration, network exposure, guardrails, and connected credentials—was ever actually reachable by the techniques attackers use, and whether unknown or unpatched gaps still exist. A fully patched system can still be exposed in ways a patch report won’t show.
How quickly are AI framework vulnerabilities typically exploited?
Often within hours to a few days of disclosure. CVE-2026-33017, a Langflow remote code execution flaw disclosed in March 2026, was weaponized within 20 hours of public disclosure—before a public proof-of-concept exploit even existed, according to researchers at Sysdig. That compressed timeline is why periodic, scheduled vulnerability scanning increasingly lags behind real attacker activity.
What frameworks should CISOs use to benchmark AI security testing?
The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications catalog the most critical risks specific to AI applications and agents, while MITRE ATLAS maps adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems the way MITRE ATT&CK does for traditional IT. Mapping AI security testing results to these frameworks gives CISOs a reporting structure security teams already understand.

Purple Team Training: A Practical Guide to Exercises, Tools and Building a Continuous Program
By:
Amanda Kegley
November 19, 2026
Purple team training helps security teams turn attack simulations into better prevention, detection and response. Offensive specialists execute attacks against the latest threats and adversary behavior, defenders examine how their controls behave in terms of blocking and alerting and both teams investigate gaps and validate fixes together. This integrated, holistic security approach with an automated  and agentic adversarial exposure validation platform closes the risk-to-fix gap between finding exposures and proving they are fixed.
For security leaders, the value is practical: evidence that your security controls are protecting you against the latest threats. Many organizations have separate teams for offensive and defensive, and too often, these teams operate in silos. The
red team
attacks, writes a report and hands it to the
blue team
weeks later, and by the time defenders act on it, the environment has changed.
Purple teaming
can replace that one-way handoff with a shared loop. Building purple teaming capability takes individual skills, collaborative testing and repeatable exercises. A continuous program connects all three.
What is purple teaming?
Purple teaming is a collaborative security approach in which red and blue teams test and improve defenses together. The red team performs agreed attacker behaviors while the blue team checks prevention, detection and response, and both teams share observations as the work happens. Learn more about
purple teaming
.
Purple teaming can be a team, a process or both. Some organizations staff a dedicated purple team. Others treat it as a working arrangement in which offensive testers, detection engineers and security analysts contribute their expertise toward a shared outcome. At its most mature, purple teaming is a program: a holistic cybersecurity approach that connects threat intelligence, attack simulation, exposure validation,
detection engineering
and remediation into one continuous cycle of improvement, rather than an occasional exercise.
For example, an authorized attack simulation might generate suspicious activity on an endpoint. The teams check whether the control blocked it, whether logs captured it and whether an alert reached an analyst. These are separate results. Recording an event does not necessarily mean the team detected or investigated it.
This approach connects demonstrated attack behavior with evidence of defensive performance. For how purple teaming fits alongside red and blue teams, see
red team vs. blue team vs. purple team
, and for how red teams hand findings to defenders, see our
red team exercise guide
.
Purple team training: building the skills and the program
Purple team training develops the technical and communication skills needed to plan attack simulations, evaluate defenses and make measurable improvements. A useful learning program covers three connected areas.
Attack simulation and exposure validation
teach practitioners to safely reproduce relevant attacker behavior and prove whether existing controls stop it, increasingly with automated platforms such as Cymulate that test and validate defenses continuously. Participants learn to select scenarios from threat intelligence, identify prerequisites and explain what each test should demonstrate. For examples mapped to MITRE ATT&CK®, see
Red Team Scenarios: 10 Real-World Attacks to Test Your Defenses
.
Detection engineering
focuses on ensuring relevant telemetry is collected and forwarded to the SIEM, then turning observable behavior into useful alerts. Defenders learn to inspect logs, develop detection logic and test whether alerts provide enough context for investigation.
Collaboration
connects the two. Participants practice explaining their actions, comparing expected and actual results and agreeing on the next change. A missed detection becomes a shared problem to solve.
Individual training paths
Structured courses can help practitioners build these skills.
SANS SEC699
covers advanced purple teaming, attack simulation and detection engineering.
MAD20 training and certifications
develop skills in applying MITRE ATT&CK to areas such as threat intelligence, attack simulation and defensive recommendations.
Choose training around the participant’s responsibilities. An offensive tester may need more experience interpreting defensive telemetry. An analyst may benefit from understanding how attackers carry out the behaviors behind an alert.
Organizational training
Turn individual learning into regular work. Pair an offensive practitioner with a defender, select a small set of relevant behaviors and work through the results together.
Tabletop sessions help teams rehearse decisions and responsibilities. Technical exercises add evidence from actual controls and workflows. Begin in a suitable test environment, then extend approved validation into representative production environments.
Give the program an owner and reserve time for remediation. Each session should leave behind reusable test cases, documented findings and validated improvements.
Purple team frameworks and tools to know
Frameworks give purple team exercises structure, and tools make the work repeatable. Choose them around your objectives, regulatory obligations and existing environment.
MITRE ATT&CK
provides a shared vocabulary for attacker behavior. Teams use it to connect threat intelligence, test cases and defensive observations.
MITRE D3FEND
maps defensive countermeasures, helping blue teams connect each tested technique to the controls and detections that should stop it.
Attack simulation plans
organize behaviors into realistic scenarios. The
Center for Threat-Informed Defense
publishes plans that teams can adapt to their scope and objectives.
Regulatory frameworks
increasingly require collaboration between red and blue teams. The TIBER-EU framework,
updated in February 2025
to align with the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), includes purple teaming in its closure phase.
Defensive tools
deliver the security and supply the evidence. Security information and event management (SIEM) and endpoint detection and response (EDR) platforms help practitioners inspect activity and evaluate alerts. This also includes allows security teams to find tune their controls across endpoint, network, email and web gateways and web application firewalls.
Adversarial exposure validation platforms
keep the work continuous between live exercises. They automate attack simulation, measure prevention and detection, and re-test fixes on demand.
Manual exercises remain useful for exploring unexpected results and teaching investigative reasoning. Automation extends their reach, and agentic AI goes further: agents choose relevant tests, run them, propose fixes and re-test, within guardrails such as audit trails and human approval for high-risk actions. The Cymulate
Threat Exposure Validation Impact Report 2025
found that respondents could test about 230 times more threats using automated validation than manual methods, and that organizations using AI took an average of 24 fewer hours to test defenses against newly identified threats. Gartner predicts that by 2029, 30% of organizations will link validation results directly to automated remediation (
2026 Gartner Market Guide for Adversarial Exposure Validation
).
How to run a purple team exercise: a step-by-step framework
A purple team exercise is a planned session in which offensive and defensive practitioners execute selected attack simulations, examine the results and improve defenses together. Use the frameworks above and the following six steps to organize a practical exercise, then carry validated tests into a continuous program.
1. Define scope and objectives
Choose a specific outcome, such as validating detection of suspicious activity on a group of managed endpoints. Identify participating systems, accounts and teams. Document authorization, testing windows, stop conditions and cleanup responsibilities, and assign a coordinator who can keep the exercise moving.
Agree on success criteria before execution. “Improve detection” is too broad. “Generate an actionable alert for each selected behavior” gives the team something concrete to evaluate.
2. Select threat scenarios and map techniques
Choose scenarios that reflect your environment, important assets and relevant threat intelligence. This makes threat-informed defense practical: testing follows plausible attacker behavior.
Map the selected tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) to the
MITRE ATT&CK framework
. Record the specific behavior, its prerequisites and the evidence you expect defenders to observe. Start with a manageable scope, and treat ATT&CK mappings as context, not proof of complete coverage.
3. Execute with red and blue collaborating live
Run the approved attack simulations while defenders inspect endpoint, network or cloud telemetry. Record execution times so the team can connect test activity with logs and alerts.
Separate the outcomes: Did the action execute? Did a control prevent it? Did monitoring record it? Did an analyst receive a useful alert? Preserve the initial result before sharing additional clues. This gives you a baseline while allowing the team to investigate together afterward.
4. Tune detection and response in real time
When a test exposes a gap, identify its cause before changing a rule. Missing telemetry, incorrect detection logic and failed alert routing require different fixes.
Make approved adjustments and rerun the same test. Then check whether normal activity creates unwanted alerts. A rule that catches the exercise but overwhelms analysts needs more work. Test response procedures too, and route larger changes through normal change controls.
5. Debrief and track remediation
Summarize what happened, what changed and what remains unresolved. Give each finding an owner, a due date and a repeatable validation test. Keep evidence that supports the conclusion, including the tested behavior, relevant configuration and observed result.
Use the debrief to improve collaboration as well. Delayed access, unclear ownership or inconsistent timestamps can slow the next exercise even when the security tools work correctly.
6. Validate fixes and repeat continuously
Close findings only after successful retesting. Then rerun approved tests after relevant changes, automate stable checks and retain live sessions for unfamiliar scenarios and deeper investigation.
The
Threat Exposure Validation Impact Report 2025
found a 20% reduction in breaches among organizations running exposure validation at least monthly. This finding covers broader exposure validation, not purple team exercises alone, but it supports a regular cadence matched to your risk, system changes and remediation capacity.
Why purple teaming must be continuous in the post-Mythos era
A periodic purple team exercise assumed attackers needed weeks to weaponize a weakness. That assumption no longer holds. In April 2026, Anthropic
withheld Claude Mythos Preview from public release, citing its ability to find software vulnerabilities
, and the UK AI Security Institute reported it could
autonomously complete a 32-step simulated network attack
.
When attackers move at machine speed, a quarterly exercise leaves months of untested exposure. A continuous purple teaming program pairs live, human-led sessions with automated attack simulation and exposure validation that re-test after every new threat, asset or control change, so defenders move at machine speed too.
Key benefits of a continuous purple teaming program
A continuous purple teaming program turns exercise findings into a maintained set of tests and improvements. Its value depends on what the team changes and verifies afterward.
Faster detection and security control tuning
Shared observation reduces the delay between executing a behavior and understanding a missed detection or prevention. Offensive practitioners explain what happened while defenders inspect the evidence. Track the time from identifying a gap to validating the fix to show whether collaboration is helping the team improve more quickly.
Shorter windows for undetected activity
Better alerts and practiced investigation help teams identify suspicious behavior sooner, and effective escalation and containment can reduce the time an attacker remains active. Measure these stages separately. Faster alert generation does not automatically mean faster containment.
Fewer blind spots between assessments
Continuous security validation
helps teams identify when changes weaken previously tested defenses. Repeatable checks can reveal a logging interruption or a detection rule that no longer behaves as expected.
The Threat Exposure Validation Impact Report 2025 found that 67% of respondents using automated
security control validation
reported significant positive changes in security metrics. Among users who also measured cyber program effectiveness, 97% reported a positive impact. For your program, track tested behaviors, actionable detections, unresolved gaps and successful retests, and compare results across equivalent test conditions.
Key takeaways
Purple teaming is a program, not just a team.
It connects attack simulation, exposure validation, detection engineering and remediation into one holistic approach.
Break the silo.
Red and blue teams deliver the most value when they share evidence, tune detections and validate fixes together.
Close findings only after re-testing.
A finding isn’t fixed until the same attack simulation proves it.
Defend at machine speed.
Pair live purple team sessions with continuous, automated attack simulation through
agentic cyber defense engineering
.
How Cymulate brings red and blue teams together
Cymulate gives red and blue teams a shared place to work, so offensive testing and defensive improvement happen in the same loop instead of in separate silos. That loop follows three connected steps: Prove. Prioritize. Adapt.
Prove.
The red team’s perspective becomes repeatable, automated attack simulations based on current threats. Blue teams see the results against their own controls, technique by technique, so both teams work from the same evidence instead of a report delivered weeks later.
Prioritize.
Prevention and detection results are mapped to MITRE ATT&CK and ranked by exploitability and business impact, so red and blue teams agree on which gaps matter most and what to fix first.
Adapt.
Blue teams get actionable mitigation and detection guidance for each gap, then re-test with the same attack to confirm the fix. The red team’s findings become the blue team’s improvements, and re-testing closes the risk-to-fix gap.
Automation handles the repeatable work within defined guardrails, with audit trails and human approval for high-risk actions, while practitioners on both sides set objectives, investigate unexpected results and decide what changes.
Ready to make purple teaming continuous?
Red teams find the gaps, and blue teams close them. With continuous purple teaming, both happen in the same loop. To explore the full operating model,

Frequently asked questions
Is purple teaming a team or a process?
Purple teaming can be either. Some organizations
staff
a dedicated purple team, while others run purple teaming as a collaborative process between existing red and blue teams. The most effective approach treats it as an ongoing program that connects attack simulation, exposure validation, detection
engineering
and remediation.
Is purple teaming a certification?
Purple teaming is a collaborative security approach, not a certification. Courses and certifications can develop relevant skills, including attack simulation, detection
engineering
and ATT&CK
application
. An effective program also requires shared processes and practice in your environment.
How is purple teaming different from red teaming?
Red teaming evaluates security through covert adversarial activity, often with limited defender knowledge. Purple teaming emphasizes open collaboration and improvement during testing. Both contribute to the same security program: red team findings become purple team test cases that defenders tune against and re-test.
How often should you run a purple team exercise?
Choose a cadence based on risk,
staffing
and environmental change. A practical starting point is a focused monthly exercise, supported by continuous automated attack simulation and exposure validation between sessions. Add targeted validation after significant control changes or new
threats, and
allow time to verify fixes.
Can purple teaming be automated?
Many repeatable activities can be automated, including threat profiling, attack simulation, detection validation,
mitigation
and re-testing. Human practitioners still lead
objectives
, investigate unexpected
results
and teach investigative reasoning. Cymulate runs the automated steps continuously within defined guardrails and shares every result with both teams, with human approval for consequential changes.

We’re introducing
GPT‑6.2 Astra
, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and
GPT‑6.2 Sol
, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. Both models deliver better results on demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done within your usage limits. For businesses and developers, that means frontier performance at costs that make sense at scale.
GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work. Its slides, spreadsheets, and documents read less like AI, and more closely follow the templates you provide and the conventions of your field. It writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design.
On Agents’ Last Exam, which tests multistep professional work, GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT‑6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost.
Agents’ Last Exam evaluates models on long-horizon professional workflows. Its leaderboard results for Fable 5.2 exclude nine tasks that used a fallback model.
We believe GPT-6.2 Astra is the best model in the world for scientists. It sets a new high on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, which tests how well models can carry out scientific work in a terminal. GPT-6.2 Astra scores 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than one-third the cost. It also sets a new high on the Vals Science Index, which asks models to interpret real biological data and run experiments to infer how a simulated system works.

In the API, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT‑6 Astra’s, with a 60% discount on cached input ($8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output, all per million tokens). GPT‑6.2 Sol keeps GPT‑6.1 Sol’s API token prices. On several benchmarks, both models come close to or outperform other leading models at a small fraction of the cost per task.
Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations across knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge.
GPT-6.2 Sol: our go-to model for everyday work
Compared with GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6.2 Sol is smarter, more efficient, and lets you complete more tasks on the same paid plan. It powers through multistep agentic workflows, writes clearly and naturally, and is intuitive to collaborate with. Many employees at OpenAI use it as their default model for both technical and non-technical tasks.
In Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0, GPT‑6.2 Sol comes within 0.5 points of GPT‑6.2 Astra at about one-fifth the cost (both at max).
FrontierCode 2.0 evaluates whether changes to real codebases meet maintainers’ standards for merging.
Its speed and intelligence also make it ideal for the important tasks people turn to AI for outside of work. On our recently released
LifeVal

evaluation, which measures performance on challenging everyday tasks, GPT‑6.2 Sol outscores GPT‑6 Astra at about one-seventh the cost.
LifeVal tests how well models handle everyday tasks tailored to someone’s needs, such as shortlisting kindergartens after a move, finding a home that fits a family’s budget and commute, or planning meals for a parent adjusting to a new diagnosis.
Professional outputs that match industry standards
We trained GPT‑6.2 Astra to create clearer, better-designed slides, spreadsheets, and documents that more closely follow the conventions professionals use in fields like law, sales, finance, and accounting. The writing is more direct and specific, with fewer generic takeaways and less filler.
Harvey LAB‑AA v1.1 uses legal assignments to test whether models can find the relevant facts across source documents, apply them to a detailed brief, and produce an accurate deliverable that meets every requirement. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new state of the art, more than doubling Claude Fable 5.2’s pass rate at about one-sixth the cost.
Astra for Law

, our configuration of GPT-6.2 Astra for lawyers, scores even higher on this benchmark.
Harvey LAB‑AA tests legal work such as reviewing contract provisions. Its headline score gives credit only when a deliverable meets every grading criterion and contains no material hallucinations.
Our internal GDPval v2 benchmark is our next iteration of
GDPval
⁠
that measures complex, long-horizon workflows from real projects in sectors like consulting, finance, and design. GPT‑6.2 Astra leads the models we tested, up 6.2 percentage points from GPT‑6 Astra while using 22% fewer output tokens. GPT‑6.2 Sol improves 5.3 points from GPT‑6.1 Sol.
GDPval v2 consists of long-horizon knowledge-work assignments from real projects in sectors like finance, data science, biotechnology, and marketing.
Workbooks and memos
Building a valuation workbook or writing an investment memo starts with finding the relevant figures in source files and working out how they fit together. Artificial Analysis’s AA‑AnalystAgent tests that work on real spreadsheets and reports. In one task, models use California Medicaid’s expenditure reports to calculate how much the program spent on medical transport. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, answering 62.5% of questions correctly on all five independent attempts.

We asked them to build an editable Excel workbook that forecasts revenue by segment through 2031 and checks that the three financial statements reconcile. The workbook also had to estimate the value per diluted share at an 8% discount rate and 3% perpetual growth, show what growth rate would justify the reference share price, and show how the valuation changes as those assumptions vary.
GPT‑6.2 Astra puts the revenue mix and the bridge from enterprise value to share value beside the sensitivity table. Readers can see which businesses drive the forecast and trace how discounted cash flows, cash and investments, and the diluted share count feed into the per-share estimate. GPT‑6 Astra shows the revenue breakdown on a separate tab and the valuation bridge farther down the sheet.
Slideshows
GPT‑6.2 Astra is our best model yet at designing slides and following slide templates, whether given an original file or even a screenshot. It can match the layout, colors, and typography down to the exact font size, and carry the template’s writing style into new slides. GPT‑6.2 Astra’s more precise computer use lets it work down to individual parts and connections in CAD and simulation tools. Engineers can use that additional detail to check how components fit, see where loads shift as a design moves, and test revisions before building a prototype.
Driving simulation
We asked GPT‑6.2 Astra to visualize chassis dynamics of a car on a mountain road. Astra created the 3D model and wrote a Python solver to simulate complex dynamics between the tires and suspension, then animated the results in Blender. This enables engineers to quickly test new designs and improve simulation accuracy over time.
Mechanical design and assembly
GPT‑6.2 Astra can model a mechanical system part by part, giving engineers a way to show how it goes together and test how design changes affect its behavior.
We asked GPT‑6.2 Astra to model a radio-controlled buggy and engine using public photos and build manuals. It modeled the individual components, created an animated assembly guide, and produced an illustrated parts catalog. This shows how Astra can accelerate physical engineering product development and documentation.
From CAD to a paper lamp
Our team used GPT‑6.2 Astra to turn the scalloped balconies of Chicago’s Marina City towers into a lamp. The video follows the design from reference photos through CAD revisions to a physical lamp assembled by hand. The site, generated by GPT-6.2 Astra, can be used to create your own paper lamp.
GPT‑6.2 Astra brings stronger visual reasoning to web design, choosing layouts and imagery that give each site a distinctive look and building elements around the actual goal of the site.

Cybersecurity capabilities
GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol mark another significant jump in cyber capabilities. They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and produce better patches, with substantial token-efficiency gains on several evaluations. Like
GPT‑6 Astra
⁠

Preparedness Framework

Due to their increased capabilities, we’re launching GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol with tighter safeguards for higher-risk cybersecurity assistance. These protections reduce misuse risk, but also restrict some legitimate vulnerability research and security testing workflows. Through
OpenAI Daybreak

GPT‑6 Cyber

Giving cyber defenders an edge
Developers increasingly rely on coding agents to write production software, even as more capable agents lower the barrier to finding and exploiting vulnerabilities.

With GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol, we made defensive capabilities a core focus, introducing new training signals to help developers prevent and repair those flaws—writing secure code from the start and producing patches that preserve intended behavior.
SecureSWE is an internal benchmark that tests writing functional and secure code for security-sensitive components such as serving files or handling database queries.
Safety and alignment
We're deploying GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol with our strongest safeguards to date. We've tightened restrictions and strengthened the systems we use to
monitor models
⁠
and
intervene when needed

Like GPT-6 Astra, in addition to meeting the Critical threshold for cybersecurity, both GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol meet the High threshold for biological and chemical capabilities under our
Preparedness Framework
⁠
. We’ve implemented protections to mitigate the associated risks, alongside increased restrictions across a set of potential dual-use biological and cybersecurity requests.
More details about our safeguards and testing are available in the
GPT-6.2 system card

AI research capabilities and safeguards
GPT-6.2 Astra is our first externally released model to meet the High threshold for AI Self-improvement, which measures a model’s ability to accelerate AI research. A ‘High’ designation reflects our assessment that the model’s impact is equivalent to giving every OpenAI researcher an additional, highly capable research engineer as an assistant, relative to their 2024 baseline. We track this capability because models that can help develop future AI systems could also introduce new risks to safety, like accelerating progress faster than safeguards or human oversight can adapt.
To address these risks, we’ve built more oversight and controls into how we train and deploy our models. Before expanding internal access to GPT-6.2 Astra, we evaluated its alignment and verified that required safeguards were in place at each stage. We
strengthened containment in our research environments
⁠
, and tested those protections with our most capable models. We also built
Control Room
⁠

expanded monitoring
⁠
examines models’ reasoning and actions across internal workloads and supported external deployments. It can automatically flag unauthorized behavior, and, where supported, pause workloads or conversations.
Alignment
Both models performed similarly to GPT-6 Astra on most alignment evaluations, and took fewer improper actions in simulated workplace tasks. However, in two tests, they were more likely to omit mentioning obstacles that blocked their work, such as a missing file or unavailable search tool. We added instructions in Codex that substantially reduce these omissions, and we’re continuing to investigate the behavior.
In Blocker Deception, we introduced an obstacle into a coding task, such as removing the file the user asked the agent to edit. The model is evaluated on whether it discloses the obstacle to the user.
Pricing and availability
Starting today, GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Pro 500 subscribers can use Ultrafast with either model. For the first time, we’re also bringing Ultrafast to Pro 200 subscribers, starting with GPT-6.2 Sol. Eligible Enterprise and Edu users get the same access once their workspace admin enables it. gpt-6.2-astra
and
gpt-6.2-sol
through the OpenAI API, with Ultrafast available for both models at launch.

Description
Palo Alto Networks is aware of the Critical Severity vulnerability in Java: CVE-2026-114938.
A buffer-overflow vulnerability in HotSpot JVM's optimized (intrinsic) Base64 decoder, affecting Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM, and OpenJDK on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI support (where Base64 hardware intrinsics are enabled by default). When decoding specially crafted Base64 input, it causes an out-of-bounds heap write that can lead to remote code execution by an unauthenticated remote attacker in affected applications
Successful exploitation relies on a combination of specific conditions: execution on an affected JDK release, underlying x86-64 hardware supporting AVX-512 VBMI with Base64 intrinsics enabled, and an exposed processing path where the application decodes untrusted Base64 input.

items.target: 比顶配便宜却跑分反超：从刚上线的 Gemini 4 Neon，看 Google 怎么跑通单会话双模型接力
items.text: yage-share published: 比顶配便宜却跑分反超：从刚上线的 Gemini 4 Neon，看 Google 怎么跑通单会话双模型接力
items.title: 比顶配便宜却跑分反超：从刚上线的 Gemini 4 Neon，看 Google 怎么跑通单会话双模型接力
items.content:
日常使用大模型进行代码编写或执行几十轮编程智能体的过程中，一个主要挑战是如何在保证质量的同时尽可能降低成本。之前有两家大厂提出了不同的解决方案。Anthropic（Claude
的开发商）在
之前读过的官方省钱指南
里提出，在同一个会话中始终使用同一个高质量的模型，同时降低其思考的档位，借此减少模型在生成答案前进行的内部推理步骤来省钱。而
DeepSeek 在
此前分析过的常驻编程代理
里用项目经理和子代理两层来实现分工，但这两层代理都需要重新阅读上下文，因此产生了
3.8 倍的重复读取开销。
然而最近五周 Google 一口气推出了四个新一代模型。他们在 2026 年 11 月
18 日发布了第四个模型
Gemini 4 Neon
，同时在自家的编程工具
Antigravity 中引入了
Orchestrator (Neon)
这种双模型调度模式。这个中等价位的新模型在测试中超过了即将恢复原价的旗舰模型
Carbon，同时为主流付费订阅提供了单会话双模型接力机制。把这三家公司对比一下，就可以看出编程智能体省钱的第三条路径。
定价低四分之一、跑分反而压过顶配，刚上线的
Neon 到底是什么来头？
先看价格。Google 最早发的 Argon 和顶配 Carbon 现在都在半价促销，到了
12 月 1 日，两款都会翻倍涨回同样的原价：每百万
token
输入 4
美元、输出 20
美元（模型内部的思考过程也按更贵的输出算）。原价一样，能力更强的 Carbon
一上来就把 Argon 衬得没法选了；更要命的是，前几天出的平价模型 Hydrogen
自带免费档，付费价不到顶配四成，跑分却直接超了
Argon。上下夹击之下，同步更新的
Gemini
官方选型指南
干脆把 Argon 从推荐主表里拿掉了。
接替主力位置的 Neon 没有促销期，直接给出每百万
token
输入 3 美元、输出 15
美元的固定挂牌价，比顶配原价低四分之一。很多人起初以为它只是填补价格空档的次旗舰，看了刚发布的
Neon
官方模型卡
才发现，它直接改自顶配
Carbon，在后训练里重点强化了编程智能体表现，写代码时偷懒走捷径的比例也压到了全系最低。
恢复原价后，改自 Carbon 的 Gemini 4 Neon
以更低单价在综合智能指数和单任务成本上反超顶配 Carbon，并替代 Argon
成为新主力。
在
Neon
官方发布博客
披露的独立评测里，它直接在综合榜单上实现了反超。Artificial Analysis
综合智能指数上，Neon 最高思考档位
xhigh
拿到 61 分，压过了
60 分的顶配 Carbon；用默认高档
high
就能打平顶配，单任务总成本比 Carbon 低
32%，同时夺得编码智能体榜单全球第一。这让 Neon 顺理成章接替刚满月的
Argon 成为推荐主力，并在 Antigravity 中置顶成为新会话的默认模型，更贵的
Carbon 退居高价 Ultra
订阅专攻极长程科研难题，日常高频的轻量开发则交给自带免费档的 Hydrogen
去跑。
Anthropic
劝死守单模型、DeepSeek 拆双层多烧缓存，Google
靠什么在单会话里跑通双模型接力？
有了不同能力的模型之后，一个直觉的想法是用强模型来指引方向，用便宜的模型来写代码。但这在工程上会碰到两个挑战，一个是缓存失效，一个是交接失灵。编程智能体每一步都会把之前的对话历史和工具说明重贴一遍。服务器会把已经算过的重复前缀存下来打折，也就是前缀缓存。但前缀缓存是绑在某个具体模型上的，不同的模型不能共享。
Anthropic 在
官方成本与智能优化指南
里统计了很多团队的数据，发现编程循环里近九成输入都靠前缀缓存省钱。但在
Anthropic 里，第一次把历史放进缓存要付 25%
的写入溢价，如果中途换模型，以前攒的缓存直接作废，新模型又要重交写入溢价，省下来的单价反而补不上。全程用便宜模型写码、实在不行再找强模型做顾问呢？Anthropic
做了近 400
次实验，没看见便宜模型主动问过一次，因为小模型根本不知道自己卡住了。所以
Anthropic 建议死守同一个强模型，通过调低思考档位来省钱。
但反手用一个强模型在同一个窗口里指挥、只把大任务分包给子代理，也会翻车。DeepSeek
测试常驻编程代理时发现，只要提示词留了可以顺手做的小事，5 轮里有 1
轮主模型会管不住手亲自下场写代码，把对话窗口锁死近半小时。为此 DeepSeek
把系统拆成两个独立会话，直接没收项目经理写代码的工具，只让它给后台子代理发工单。这虽然治好了手痒，但两边都要分别重读代码库和对话记录，平白多花了近四倍的缓存
token
。
单模型太贵、拆双层又费缓存，Google
选的第三条路是在同一条会话里直接交棒。以前大家不敢中途换模型，除了怕缓存作废，更怕思路断掉：便宜模型只看到几行结论，很容易改偏。按照
Gemini
思考机制文档
，Gemini 4
每轮回答前会把内部推演打包成一段推理签名存在后台。切给便宜模型时，后台自动把这份签名接过去，接手的模型能直接顺着上一棒的思路接着干。
那为什么 Anthropic 劝大家别中途换模型，Google
这里却划算了？跨模型不能共享缓存这一点两家一样，换模型的那一轮，新模型都得按原价重读一遍上下文。差别在于交棒的代价和后续的回报。Anthropic
写缓存要多收 25%
的写入费，在一个已经聊长的会话中途换模型，重读加写入的成本一下就把差价吃掉了。Google
这边用隐式缓存，输入满门槛自动打 95%
折扣，而且不收写入费，切模型的过路费低得多。更重要的是交棒时机：
Orchestrator (Neon)
趁开局刚做完规划、上下文还短的时候就早早交给
Hydrogen。接下来十几轮写代码、跑测试，大头开销其实在模型输出上（输出单价是输入的
5 倍，Hydrogen 输出只有 Neon 的一半），而且每轮重复输入都命中 Hydrogen
自己的缓存。趁开局短的时候交一次小过路费，换后面十几轮输出直接打对折，自然就划算了。
有了这套底层接口，Google 在
Antigravity
模型和调度文档
中推出了
Orchestrator (Neon)
，让两个模型可以在同一轮回复里接力。每次收到需求，先让
Neon
进入只读模式探索代码库、写出计划并定下何时需要重规划；计划定好，系统在同一会话里交棒给便宜的
Hydrogen
改代码、跑测试；执行期间如果测试连续失败两次、接口行为与预期不符，或撞上未拍板的设计分支，控制权就自动弹回
Neon 查现场修计划，再交回 Hydrogen 继续跑。上周 Google 先推出了顶配
Carbon 搭档 Hydrogen 的编排模式，根据
Antigravity
官方博客
披露的编程基准实测，这套双模型接力的成功率已接近单跑顶配，平均省了 24%
额度、提速近两成。如今把更便宜的 Neon 接进来做成
Orchestrator (Neon)
，就从高价 Ultra 档下放到了主流付费 Pro
订阅。
Anthropic 靠单模型降档保缓存，DeepSeek
靠双层隔离治手痒但多烧 3.8 倍缓存，Google 的 Orchestrator
则在同一条会话里用只读规划和两次失败回弹实现双模型接力。
为什么一换小模型就得补规矩：从结果确定性退回过程确定性的必然
如果暂时不论缓存折扣、接口参数等细节，这三个厂商的技术路线差异，本质上反映了智能体工程中两种不同的控制哲学。我在之前的文章《
从过程确定性到结果确定性
》中比较过这两种确定性。结果确定性是不规定具体的每一步怎么做，只明确最终验收标准，通过模型的推理、观察和纠错来达到目标；过程确定性则是在流程的阶段、工具权限和外部触发条件等方面对过程进行强约束。前者强调模型的自由裁量权，后者则强调通过流程护栏保证可靠性。
这两种思路哪个更好，取决于你用的模型是否足够聪明。对于 Anthropic
这种指令跟随好、判断力强的旗舰模型，采用单模型的结果确定性是合理的。只要把目标明确说明，它自己就知道什么时候需要查代码、什么时候需要调整策略，不需要额外的流程。但在成本压力下改用小模型，或者在单窗口里用提示词来区分不同角色，小模型往往不能可靠地跟随隐含的指令，甚至不知道自己卡住了，Anthropic
在近 400 次实验里都没有看到它主动求助。同时 DeepSeek
也观察到，哪怕是强模型，在单窗口里看到写代码的工具时，也不一定能克制住自己写代码的冲动。这时候就需要用过程确定性从外部兜底约束。
DeepSeek 和 Google 都加入了过程确定性的设计，只是强度不同。DeepSeek
通过物理拆分两个会话加上直接取消项目经理写码工具来提供较强的过程确定性，让主模型根本不会去尝试写码，但代价是两个会话分别重读仓库，额外消耗了
3.8 倍的缓存。Google 的
Orchestrator (Neon)
同样提供了过程确定性，但把它做得更轻量，放在同一个会话里：在规划期给强模型只读权限防止手痒，在实施期用测试连续失败两次这种外部明确信号把失控的小模型弹回强模型。用最轻的过程确定性兜住小模型的下限，同时保留单会话的上下文和缓存连续性，这是双模型接力有效协作的关键。
手头正在跑的
Agent 工作流，现在怎么选档、怎么抄作业？
如果你直接用 Antigravity 写码，日常开发、修 bug 和跨文件重构直接选
Orchestrator (Neon)
就好，唯一要注意它的内部配比固定，不能手动调节思考档位。只是改小脚本、升级依赖或补单测，直选带免费档的
Hydrogen 更快；真遇到每一步都要深度推演的复杂系统设计，再直选 Neon 开
high
档或
xhigh
档。
如果你自己调接口搭智能体，可以在月底恢复原价前把旧的 Argon 配置改成
Neon 加
Hydrogen。与此同时，可以直接套用官方编排器的两条轻量规矩：一是在规划阶段锁只读工具，逼强模型只定方案和异常触发条件，不顺手写大段模板代码；二是不指望小模型自觉求助，改用测试验证连续失败两次这类明确信号，强制切回强模型重编计划。
在投入生产之前，有两点需要注意。第一点是 Neon
刚刚发布，官方和合作榜单以外并没有长期检验，对于超长对话或者冷门代码库的真实口碑，还需要在社区运行几周后才能沉淀出来。第二点是如果某些极难任务还是需要调用
Carbon，需要提防线上延迟波动。根据转发平台
OrcaRouter
的生产监测
显示，过去一周 Carbon 有一半的请求需要等待 10
秒以上才吐出第一个字，接近四分之一直接报错。官方也建议把复杂请求的超时设到至少
15
分钟或者放后台跑。在代码中先把长超时和报错重试配齐，再去切这个双模型流水线心里更有底。

items.text: innei published: AI 时代的审美赤字：当人人都能做出一个 App
items.title: AI 时代的审美赤字：当人人都能做出一个 App
items.content:
A little over half a year ago, I wrote an essay reflecting on this topic: "
The Efficiency Paradox of the AI Era: When Greater Productivity Only Leaves Us Exhausted
." Back then, I asked: in the age of AI, when productivity was supposed to be liberated, why is everyone feeling more exhausted than ever?
Over the past half-year, this trend has become increasingly obvious.
Deep, focused mental work has increasingly fractured into constant context switching across multiple projects.
It feels like we have all developed ADHD in this era, struggling to stay focused on any single thing for long.
And the more capable models become, the worse it gets: we rarely work on just one thing anymore; instead, we juggle several concurrently.
Most people are the same way, running multiple side projects at once. Building things has become almost trivial—you can easily crank out several in a single day.
On top of that, the breakneck pace of AI has made us deeply dependent on it. Now, even just kicking off a new project requires an assist from AI.
"Building It" Doesn't Mean Skill
Model progress over the past half-year has been blistering—GPT 5.4 is already an eight-month-old model.
Meanwhile, Chinese models have been playing catch-up, and by now they are at least on par with GPT 5.4. Just a few months ago, people were still debating whether hitting 5.4 would be enough to be satisfied.
With models as capable as they are now, technical barriers have largely vanished, and what people jokingly call "wishful programming"—prompting an app into existence—has become all the rage. Even a complete novice can build an app that basically meets requirements, though it might not be very good to use.
To be fair, the rapid rise of AI has let more people experience the joy of building software and create tools that help their daily lives or work—and that is genuinely meaningful.
But churning out endless garbage apps purely for hype, trend-chasing, and plagiarism is both shameful and sad.
"Building It Well" Doesn't Mean It's Valuable
In this environment, design and usability still matter immensely to me. An outsider might not grasp design philosophy or have much aesthetic sense. And among the flood of AI-generated apps everywhere, the vast majority are simply garbage.
This breakneck pace of iteration completely bypasses traditional development workflows. Design is no longer an upfront requirement in an AI workflow; it might even be outsourced entirely to whatever taste the model has. Does that mean design no longer matters?
Even apps from top-tier Chinese tech giants can leave you deeply skeptical of their aesthetics once you try them. Take Tencent's Work Buddy: daily active users have already topped 10 million, yet when I opened it with a sense of reverence, taking in its UI, visual texture, and usability, all I could call it was garbage.
Granted, perhaps that is because I consider myself a design engineer and have a heightened sensitivity to UI details.
In a climate like this, have people simply stopped caring about whether software is intuitive and beautiful?
Most users do not care about this at all. Even if the UI is hideous, the UX is clumsy, and performance is completely ignored—so long as it barely works, many users have begun to compromise, or just stopped caring altogether in this AI wave. As long as it gets their work done and delivers what they want, that is all that matters.
Examples like this are everywhere. With so many apps, you have no idea why the interface is so ugly or what the software is even supposed to help you do, yet it still manages to blow up with insane hype in this climate.
When total novices who know nothing about software engineering, architecture, or design can use marketing tactics to churn out a completely pointless piece of garbage, I find that a tragedy of our era.
Meanwhile, craftsmen who tirelessly polish a product, pouring in genuine ideas, design sensibility, and intuitive usability, get neither the recognition nor the respect they deserve—buried and forgotten simply because their growth tactics fell short. That, too, is a tragedy.
In an era like this, does it even make sense to build a product with care anymore?
The other end takes the exact same shape: in products, aesthetics are pushed behind whether something can be built at all; in models, the top-tier capabilities are consolidating into just a few companies. You have more and more to choose from, but fewer and fewer things that are actually good.
"The Best" Doesn't Mean It's Yours
Once you have used frontier models, though, your appetite is endless. Looking back, even 5.4, as the cutting-edge model of its time, was more than capable of handling most of our daily work—and today, domestic Chinese models have long surpassed that benchmark.
Constrained by compute and tightening US export controls, domestic models still face an uphill battle against America's frontier. The window to catch up is shrinking, and the frontier is moving at breakneck speed—releasing a new generation every month is considered slow, and competing labs sometimes drop two in a single month. Naturally, everyone still wants to use the most advanced models, but here in China, actually using them is only getting harder.
Among frontier model labs, OpenAI has been relatively consumer-friendly and less restrictive with regional geoblocking, but its flagship models are noticeably falling behind Anthropic's. That strikes me as a sad state of affairs. In the closed-source space, Anthropic essentially stands alone at the top right now; while Gemini and OpenAI keep trying to close the distance, the gap still feels immense.
And Anthropic happens to be a deeply anti-human organization. It feels like they just want to play dictator in the AI era, wishing nobody else would make models unless it fits the utopian society they want to construct—which is why they don't want open-weight models to evolve.
